title: Stigma, talking to family and starting therapy
question_forms: Why is therapy still taboo, and how do I start?
How do I talk to my family about mental health?
How do I heal from childhood trauma and emotional neglect?
Can I get therapy on the NHS without seeing a GP?
tradition_says: Many Black families say problems stay in the family, pray about it, or that therapy is for white people or for people who are weak.

layer1.plain_answer: A London study found stigma, silence and beliefs about causes slow help-seeking in African-descended communities, including in church groups. You can start without a diagnosis: in the UK you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies for anxiety, depression and trauma. Telling one person you trust is a first step.

do.text: Refer yourself to NHS (UK) talking therapies online if you are 18 or over and registered with a doctor; you do not need a diagnosis.
Tell one person you trust; starting the conversation is what matters.
For trauma, note that PTSD is among the problems NHS (UK) talking therapies treat by self-referral.
Ask about help through your employer, university or local charities if the UK's NHS wait is long.
Do not wait: the UK's NHS says the sooner you see a doctor about depression, the sooner you can recover.

avoid.text: Staying silent because of what the community may think: stigma and silencing were what blocked help in the London study.
Choosing a private therapist who is not registered with an accredited body.

see_someone_when: Low mood, anxiety or trauma symptoms last more than a couple of weeks or stop you functioning (doctor or NHS in the UK talking therapies self-referral).
Eating disorders, bipolar disorder, psychosis or drug and alcohol problems (doctor referral; these usually need a doctor, per NHS in the UK).

In a crisis or thinking about suicide: in the UK call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option (England), call Samaritans free on 116 123 (24 hours), or call 999 in an emergency; in the US call or text 988 or call 911.

tested.population: 26 men and women in Christian faith communities, south London
tested.design: Qualitative interviews on stigma and help-seeking for mental illness
tested.finding: Help-seeking was shaped by beliefs about the causes of mental illness, silencing driven by stigma, and stigma kept up at community level. People with a diagnosis could face triple jeopardy in stigma. The authors say one-size-fits-all approaches will not meet diverse needs.

source.authors: Mantovani N, Pizzolati M, Edge D

tested.note: Small qualitative study in one setting; shows themes, not how common they are.

tier_driver: Why stigma delays help in Black communities: one qualitative study of 26 people in faith groups in south London.
tier_note: Tier B observational (qualitative), strength thin. How to talk to family and how to heal from childhood trauma returned no source I could open, so those parts are guidance on getting a first appointment only.
harm_note: No harm signal found. The risk is staying silent, or choosing an unregistered practitioner.
evidence_summary: Mantovani, Pizzolati and Edge (2017) interviewed 26 people from Christian faith groups in south London and found stigma, silence and beliefs about causes shaped help-seeking. The UK's NHS talking therapies page says you can self-refer for anxiety, depression and PTSD without seeing a doctor, and that bipolar, psychosis, eating disorders and drug problems usually need a doctor referral. Childhood trauma and emotional neglect are not named on that page, so I cannot say it is covered by self-referral; ask the service.
gaps: Untested or not found: scripts for talking to family; trauma and emotional neglect therapy in Black adults; whether faith-based programmes improve access; UK data beyond one London study.
